JUDGMENT

_____________________________________________________________________

[1]

Plaintiff, Ms. R. N. is suing her sister in two
cases that are now joined.

[2]

JS1699

The cases are scheduled to proceed on the merits
starting on November 16, 2020, for a period of six days.

[3]

A few days ago, the parties asked the
coordinating judge for the month of November 2020 to assign them a judge to
hear some pre-hearing motions. Exceptionally, the coordinating judge agreed and
designated the undersigned.

[4]

There are four motions before the Court.

4.1.

A motion by R. N.
[1]

to obtain a copy of her late mother’s file at the CHSLD Notre-Dame-de-la-Merci
and at the Public Curator;

4.2.

A motion by the Human Rights Commission asking
to quash a summons sent to Mr. Germain Royer;

4.3.

A motion by Mr. I. H. to quash a summons sent to
him;

4.4.

A motion by Ms. Anne Lamontagne and Ms. Sophie
Gouin to quash summons served on them.

[5]

A fifth motion, presented by Ms. Patricia Raveau
to quash a summons served on her was withdrawn given that R. N. mentioned she
no longer wished to call her as a witness.

1.

BACKGROUND

[6]

The late Mi. N. and her late husband M3. N. had
two daughters, R. N. and M. H.. The family stayed in a duplex on [Street A] in Town
A.

[7]

M3. N. died in April 2000.

[8]

In December 2009, Mi. N. signed a mandate in
case of incapacity appointing R. N. as her mandatory.

[9]

In
March 2010, Mi. N. transferred two immovable in R. N.’s name, including the
duplex on [Street A]. At the same time, she signed a will appointing R. N. as
sole legatee and liquidator of her mother’s estate as well as a mandate
appointing R. N. as her representative in case of incapacity.

[10]

R. N. lived with her mother in the [Street A]
duplex until the intervention of the Human Rights Commission in 2012.

[11]

In 2009, M. H. was concerned about her mother’s
welfare. She suspected that Mi. N. was abused by R. N. She brought Mi. N. to
the Jewish General Hospital for an evaluation. The doctor concluded that Mi. N.
suffered from mild dementia. He found no evidence of abuse. Mi. N. was allowed
to return home with R. N.

[12]

M. H. remained unconvinced. In October 2010, she
called the CLSC voicing her concerns for her mother’s health. Ms. Anne
Lamontagne and Ms. Sophie Gouin (the “
Social Workers
”) were assigned to
the case by the CIUSSS du Nord-de-l’Île-de-Montréal.

a)

Parallel Judicial History

[13]

In June 2011, M. H. filed a complaint with the
Human Rights Commission. They investigated. The Commission asked Mi. N. to
submit to an evaluation. She agreed. Further to the evaluation, Mi. N. was
transferred to the CHSLD Notre-Dame-de-la-Merci.

[14]

The Public Curator asked to open a protection
regime. R. N. contested. She argued that if her mother was incapacitated (which
she denied), she should act as mandatary under the mandate signed in December
2009. The Public Curator and R. N. filed competing motions.

[15]

The Human’s Right Commission intervened.

[16]

The Public Curator’s motion and R. N.’s motion
were heard in 2014. In September 2014, after a seven-day hearing, Justice Marc De
Wever granted the Public Curator’s motion and dismissed R. N.’s. He concluded:

16.1.

That Mi. N. had the capacity to sign the mandate appointing R. N. as
mandatary in December 2009;

16.2.

That it would nonetheless not be in the interest of Mi. N. to
homologate the mandate appointing R. N. as mandatary given that R. N. does not
have her mother’s best interest at heart.

[
17
]

In 2013, after completing its investigation, the
Human Rights Commission filed proceedings alleging that Mi. N. was the victim of
exploitation between September 2009 and November 2012. The Commission sought
damages against R. N. and the annulment of the property transfers.

[
18
]

After a 13-day hearing (although it was
initially scheduled for 4 days), Justice Scott Hughes dismissed the Commission’s
claim without costs
[2]
. He concluded that:

18.1.

In December 2009, Mi. N. had the mental capacity to consent to the
donations of the properties and that she did so of her own volition (par. 257
to 272).

18.2.

R. N. provided “no satisfactory explanation” as to why Mi. N. would
have given her the immovables while in the past, she had always treated her two
daughters equally (par. 271-272).

18.3.

While certain of R. N.’s monetary transactions in her mother’s
account were “highly questionable”, these transactions were insufficient to
conclude that Mi. N. was the victim of exploitation (par. 280-281).

18.4.

M. H. had distorted or exaggerated facts (par. 282-287).

18.5.

The Social Workers and the investigator appointed by the Commission
lacked critical thinking and had too easily adopted M. H.’s point of view
without giving R. N. a chance to be heard (par. 288 to 294).

18.6.

R. N. could nonetheless not be considered a victim in this matter as
she had unduly and abusively delayed the proceedings and had herself made
statements that were found to lack sincerity (par. 295 to 299).

[
19
]

In March 2018, R. N.
filed an action in damages against the Attorney General for Québec, the
Commission, the Public Curator, the attorney acting for the Public Curator, the
CIUSSS du Nord-de-l’Île-de-Montréal, the Social Workers and others. She claimed
$1.5 million in compensatory damages and $800,000 in punitive damages.

[
20
]

In June 2019, Justice
Silvana Conte decided the claim against the Social Workers, the CIUSS and the
Public Curator was prescribed. She further held that the Commission and its
representatives benefit from immunity with regards to its investigations.
Justice Conte dismissed the case on a preliminary motion
[3]
.

b)

The Current Proceedings

[
21
]

The above facts led to two lawsuits by R. N. against
her sister:

[
22
]

In 2012, R. N. filed a claim before the Small
Claims Court seeking $7,000 in damages. In May 2015, her claim was increased to
$77,000
[4]
.

[
23
]

In 2015, R. N. filed another damage claim
alleging several statements that she alleges amount to defamation against her.
At first, she claimed $90,000. The claim was increased to $820,000 in November
2016
[5]
.

[
24
]

The two cases are now joined and are scheduled
to proceed on November 16, 2020.

[
25
]

Mi. N. died in February 2018. R. N. claims that
she was not informed and that this created additional stress and damages.

[
26
]

In December 2018, Justice Kirkland Casgrain
dismissed M. H.’s motion to dismiss both cases. He noted, however, that R. N.’s
proceedings should be tightly managed and that a detailed schedule should be filed
and adhered to by the parties.

[
27
]

In March 2019, Justice Jérôme Frappier held a
case management hearing that lasted for most of the day. Given the history of
the file, Justice Casgrain’s order and the principle of proportionality, he
determined that the witness list and the time allowed for each would be as
follows:

[
28
]

Justice Frappier further ordered the parties to
file all documents they intend to use for the trial prior to May 3, 2019.

[
29
]

In June 2019, based on Justice Frappier’s
assessment, the trial was set for six days starting on November 16, 2020.

[
30
]

The crux of R. N.’s case against her sister can
be summarized as follows:

30.1.

M. H. made false accusations against R. N. to health professionals,
the Social Workers, Commission investigators, CHSLD staff and others which
caused these various entities to treat her suspiciously and to take measures
that were detrimental to her and her mother.

30.2.

This treatment had the effect of alienating R. N. from her mother to
the point where she was no longer admitted to visit her and was not even informed
of her mother’s death.

30.3.

These actions caused her significant anguish and damages.

30.4.

As M. H. was the instigator of these actions, she should be held
liable for their consequences.

2.

Analysis

a)

Applicable Law

[
31
]

Requests for documents are an essential
component of the preliminary phase of civil cases. This exploration phase
encourages transparency, allows the issues to be defined quickly and
facilitates transactions. It is thus important to favour disclosure of any
document that will enable the parties to establish the merits of their case
[6]
.

[
32
]

However, the Supreme Court also warns that
relevance, the right to privacy and professional secrecy play a central role in
this area. The judge must take care to ensure that documents requested are
within the limits of what is relevant, that is, of what is useful for the case
[7]
.

[
33
]

Furthermore, any pre-trial order, including
those relating to document requests, must respect the philosophy put forward by
the
Code of Civil Procedure
.
[8]
This philosophy is articulated around certain guiding principles in
particular, the right to be heard (art. 17 CCP), proportionality (art. 18 CCP),
sound administration of justice and the proper conduct of proceedings (art. 19
CCP) as well as the duty of cooperation and information (art. 20 CCP). As
underlined in the preliminary provision of the C.C.P., these principles are
designed “to ensure the accessibility, quality and promptness of civil justice
[and] the fair, simple, proportionate and economical application of procedural
rules”.

[
34
]

Based on the above, courts have established a
certain number of guidelines that apply to requests for documents or motions to
quash
subpoena duces tecum
:

34.1.

Generally, a person who has useful information may be subpoenaed and
be asked to bring documents relevant to a dispute
[9]
.

34.2.

Courts have the power to intervene when a request for documents or a
subpoena is contrary to the sound administration of justice or exceeds what is
necessary to adequately resolve a dispute
[10]
.

34.3.

In particular, the Court must step in if the requested documents are
irrelevant or compliance would impose an undue burden on the party which is the
object of the request (even more so when the request is made to a third person
who is not a party to the proceedings). This will be the case when the request
is formulated in such a broad manner that it constitutes a “fishing expedition”
[11]
.

34.4.

Although a court must always be very prudent in doing so, it may be
appropriate in certain cases to dispose of the request prior to the scheduled
date of appearance especially when compliance with the request or summons
involves undue inconvenience and the weak probative value of the information
sought is manifest
[12]
.

34.5.

In all cases surrounding requests for documents, the Court must also
be mindful of the judicial contract that binds the parties. Case Protocols and
Joint declarations of readiness have been described as the cornerstone of the
legal framework within which the parties are required to evolve. This framework
was adopted to foster the full disclosure of evidence, ensure a fair debate and
avoid unnecessary postponements and delays which burden the judicial system.
Compliance with these undertakings requires litigants to prepare for their
trial in advance and avoid last-minute changes
[13]
.
While these judicial contracts should not be considered straitjackets, Courts
have not hesitated to quash requests which conflict with a joint declaration of
readiness, especially when the request comes on the eve of trial
[14]
.

b)

R. N.’s Motion to Obtain Documents

[
35
]

On October 15, 2020 (a month before the case is
scheduled to be heard) R. N. filed a motion seeking:

35.1.

A complete unredacted copy of Mi. N.’s medical file from CHSLD
Notre-Dame-de-la-Merci from January 1, 2014, to December 31, 2018; and

35.2.

A complete unredacted copy of Mi. N.’s file from the Public Curator
from January 1, 2012, to December 31, 2018.

[
36
]

She asked that these documents be provided
within three days.

[
37
]

R. N. argues that the Supreme Court of Canada
has, on numerous occasions, advocated the necessity for transparency and that
the documents are needed for her to prove the influence her sister had on the
actions taken by the CHSLD or the Public Curator.

[
38
]

The CHSLD objected. It argues that the request
is a fishing expedition, that it is presented too late and that it would be
irresponsible to further tax the resource of the CHSLD in the current pandemic
context. It adds that Mi. N.’s medical file is confidential under the
Act
respecting health services and social services
.
[15]

[
39
]

The Public Curator also objects based on the
rule of proportionality and the tardiness of the request. It adds that the
Public Curator’s file is confidential
[16]
and that the exception which allows the represented person or her
heirs to have access to the file should be interpreted restrictively. They
argue that this exception should apply when access is sought for purposes that
are not in the interest of the represented party. Finally, it mentions that it
has already provided R. N. with all the financial information necessary for her
to properly administer Mi. N.’s estate.

[
40
]

R. N.’s request for documents is overly broad
and is a perfect example of what Courts have called a fishing expedition.

[
41
]

The request spans a period of several years (5
in the case of the CHSLD and 7 in the case of the Public Curator). Her request
is not limited in any way.

[
42
]

At the hearing of the motion, R. N. proposed to
restrict her request to those portions of the file that relate to all
communications between the CHSLD (or the Public Curator) and her sister. Had
such a curtailed request been the subject of a motion prior to the declaration
of readiness, it could have been considered. However, at this stage, it cannot
be granted.

[
43
]

Imposing on the CHSLD or the Public Curator to
go through 5 or 7 years of documents to extract those that would comply with Plaintiff’s
criterion would impose an undue burden on these third parties.

[
44
]

Furthermore, R. N.’s request is in violation of
the undertakings she took when she signed the Joint declaration. At the time,
she declared that all documents she needed to proceed were in her possession
and had been filed. In his case management judgment, Justice Frappier required
the parties to file all documents they needed prior to May 3, 2019.

[
45
]

R. N. has been in litigation involving the Public
Curator and the CHSLD for many years. She is definitely aware of the existence
of these files. She has also had access to portions of them. In fact, many extracts
have been filed into the court record. Yet, she has provided no valid
explanation for her delay in presenting her motion for document requests.

[
46
]

Through her document request, R. N. is seeking
to reopen the exploratory phase of the proceeding. She surmises that something
in one of these files could potentially be useful to her to prove that M. H.
provided the CHSLD or the Public Curator with false information that induced
the CHSLD or the Public Curator to act in a certain way.

[
47
]

While the Court must be mindful of the parties’
right to present their case in a complete manner, R. N.’s late quest for
evidence that may potentially exist is not compatible with the principles of
proportionality and the sound management of judicial proceedings.

[
48
]

R. N.’s request for documents is dismissed.

[
49
]

This being said, R. N. has also sent subpoenas
to certain Public Curator representatives. The Public Curator agrees to provide
specific documents requested from those witnesses.

c)

The Human Rights Commission’s Motion to Quash

[
50
]

In support of its motion, the Human Rights
Commission relies on
section 95
of the
Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms
[17]
which states:

95.

[…]
no member or mandatary of the commission or member of
its personnel may be compelled to give testimony before a tribunal as to
information obtained in the performance of his duties or to produce a document
containing any such information, except for the purpose of ascertaining whether
it is confidential.

[
51
]

This article is rather straightforward. It has
been applied consistently by the courts to quash subpoenas issued in
contradiction with its terms
[18]
.

[
52
]

It is true that in
Fermont (ville)
v.
Québec
(Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse)
[19]
, the Court of Appeal confirmed that
article 95
of the
Charter

is not absolute. For example, the Court stated that the prohibition applied
only to those documents or elements of the investigation that have remained
confidential. It also ruled that representatives of the Commission could be
compelled to testify on the progress of the investigation resulting from the
complaint filed and to explain the circumstances which gave rise to a delay.
This being said, the Court of Appeal left no doubt that article 95 prevents a
summons to an employee of the Commission to obtain i) elements of proof
discovered during the Commission’s investigation which had not yet been disclosed
or ii) documents that refer to such elements.

[
53
]

There is no reason to depart from this
jurisprudence here.

[
54
]

Mr. Royer was, at all times relevant to the
present matter a member of the Commission. The subpoena sent by R. N. mentions
that she is seeking to obtain “email and telephone communications” that Mr.
Royer exchanged with M. H. during the course of his investigation.

[
55
]

R. N. admits that, as a result of the
proceedings filed by the Commission, she obtained some elements of the
Commission’s file. What she wishes to obtain are those communications that have
not yet been disclosed and have so far remained confidential.

[
56
]

These communications are covered by the scope of

section 95
of the
Charter
.

[
57
]

This is not to say that R. N. is barred from
adducing evidence relating to communications between M. H. and the Commission.
Such communications remain admissible. However, they cannot be proven by
summoning Mr. Royer.

[
58
]

The Human Rights Commission’s motion must be
granted.

d)

Mr. I. H.’s Motion to Quash

[
59
]

Mr. I. H. is M. H.’s husband.

[
60
]

On October 15, 2020, R. N. sent him a subpoena
asking him to bring to Court the following documents:

60.1.

Copies of his diplomas;

60.2.

Personal notes taken by him during the hearing before the Human
Rights Tribunal in December 2015;

60.3.

Bank accounts and investment statements for the years 2014 to 2019;

60.4.

Federal income tax statements for years 2014 to 2019.

[
61
]

Mr. I. H. is not a party to the present
proceedings. His work experience, his net worth or his finances have, at most,
a purely tangential relevance to the issues before the court.

[
62
]

Pressed to explain why these documents could be
relevant, R. N. mentioned that they could be used to contradict statements that
M. H. made in her discovery regarding her own standard of living.

[
63
]

The Court fails to see how M. H.’s or Mr. I. H.’s
financial health could impact the court’s decision on any of the questions
raised in R. N.’s proceedings.

[
64
]

Mr. I. H.’s Motion to Quash is granted.

e)

Motion to Quash by Ms. Anne Lamontagne and Ms.
Sophie Gouin

[
65
]

Ms. Lamontagne and Ms. Gouin are the social
workers that were assigned to Mi. N. further to M. H.’s complaint to the CLSC.

[
66
]

The Social Workers were subpoenaed by M. H. on
September 29, 2020.

[
67
]

They ask that the subpoena be quashed. They
argue that they are bound by professional secrecy obligations
[20]
which they would be obliged to breach if they were compelled to
testify.

[
68
]

It is worth mentioning that the Social Workers
have testified in the past and that portions of their reports were used both
before Justice Marc De Wever and before Justice Scott Hughes. At the time, no
one seemed to have raised professional secrecy obligations.

[
69
]

In any event, professional secrecy belongs to
the client, in this case, Mi. N.. The secrecy covers interactions with the
client. This is not the subject of the Social Workers’ intended testimony. R.
N. wants to show that M. H. tainted the views of the Social Workers by making
false statements about her. M. H. wants to show that the Social Workers came to
their own conclusions.

[
70
]

The Social Workers were intimately involved in
many relevant aspects of this matter. They evaluated Mi. N. and made
recommendations that she be moved to the CHSLD. Justice Hughes concluded that
they had several contacts with M. H. and had adopted her alarmist attitude.

[
71
]

Both of them were listed by Justice Frappier in
the witness list prepared at the time the matter was scheduled for trial.

[
72
]

Their testimony is certainly relevant.

[
73
]

The Motion to Quash by Ms. Anne Lamontagne and
Ms. Sophie Gouin is dismissed.

3.

Closing remarks

[
74
]

In order to ensure that the trial can proceed
efficiently, the Court asked that Plaintiff and Defendant’s counsel cooperate
to prepare:

74.1.

A list of exhibits they agree can be filed by consent without the
proper witness being present
